explain.say: In places like Iceland, New Zealand and California, hot rock lies unusually close to the surface. Water trapped in the rock a few kilometres down is heated to well over 150 degrees Celsius, staying liquid under great pressure.

faq.q: Where does geothermal heat come from?
faq.a: It comes from the Earth's hot interior, kept warm mostly by the slow decay of radioactive elements in the rocks, plus heat left from when the planet formed. Near volcanoes and plate edges, that heat comes close to the surface.
asks: Why is the inside of the Earth hot?

faq.q: What is a flash steam plant?
faq.a: It uses very hot water from deep underground. When the water reaches lower pressure at the surface, part of it suddenly boils, or flashes, into steam, which drives the turbine.
asks: How does hot water turn into steam in a geothermal plant?

faq.q: What is a binary geothermal plant?
faq.a: In a binary plant, the hot underground water never touches the turbine. It passes through a heat exchanger and boils a second fluid with a low boiling point, whose vapour drives the turbine, so cooler sources can still make electricity.
asks: Can geothermal work with warm water?

faq.q: Why is the water pumped back underground?
faq.a: Reinjecting the water refills the hot reservoir so it does not run dry, keeps the pressure up and safely returns the minerals and gases dissolved in it.

faq.q: Which countries use geothermal power the most?
faq.a: The United States makes the most geothermal electricity in total, but Kenya and Iceland get a much bigger share of their electricity from it: over 40 percent in Kenya and about 30 percent in Iceland.

facts: The world's first geothermal power station was built at Larderello, Italy, in 1911, after an experiment there lit light bulbs in 1904.
Geothermal power stations can run around the clock, whatever the weather.
